SL:
Weaker students used the compound interest formula inappropriately when PMT was not zero. There was confusion

Students generally used their financial application for both parts although some correctly used the compound interest
formula for part (b) and some also tried erroneously to use it in part (a). They mostly wrote the entries that they used in their
application, but they are advised to show all entries as sometimes marks were lost when important information about their
method was unavailable to the examiner. For a few students there was an issue in understanding that the 100000 EUR was
to be subtracted from FV from (a) to find the PV in (b). In part (b) there were several different possible values that could be
used for N, but these needed to be combined with the appropriate values of P/Y and C/Y which were often confused.
The principal issue with the question was with the accuracy of the answers: two decimal places was required. The range of
answers seen included full calculator display, rounding to the nearest integer and three significant figures. The term quarterly in
the question caused problems for some students although it is one that is used in the subject guide.

SL:
The majority of students performed well, although several misinterpreted part (d) by using incorrect loan values or
improperly entering data into the Finance Solver. Students generally demonstrated good understanding of the finance
application on their GDC, rarely resorting to the compound interest formula. However, issues with rounding were common in
parts (a) and (d), with answers not given either to the nearest dollar or two decimal places as required.
Students using the compound interest formula for part (b) often left their answers in years instead of months. Most students
successfully found the future value, but some did not round to two decimal places. Those using the finance solver were more

application and made it straightforward for examiners to identify any errors. In part (b) some students found their answer in
years (13.4738…) and failed to change this into months and in general, confusion over yearly and monthly periods
frequently led to a loss of marks. Some students missed the instruction to give the answer correct to the nearest dollar in part
(d) and lost marks through this oversight.

parts.report_text:
SL:
Students found this question challenging. They were not used to dealing with
piecewise functions. In part (a), they did not realize that they had to find the heights
for each value from 0 until 4, in steps of 1, in order to calculate the approximate
area under the model between 0 and 4. The trapezoidal rule appeared to be
unfamiliar to many students. The formula was copied from the formulae booklet,
but it appeared as if many students did not know how to use the formula. Many
substituted x values into the formula instead of heights. Some used an interval of 2
instead of 1. Most students misunderstood part (b). They were asked to integrate
the expression, but the majority substituted limits to find a numerical answer. Those
who did try to integrate often made mistakes or did not simplify the fractions or
omitted "c". Some differentiated the function rather than integrate it. Many students
were awarded some follow through marks in part (c) if they had evaluated the
integral correctly in part (b), but very few gave the answer as an exact value.
Students also managed to calculate the area under the curve between 4 and 5 and
5 and 12 correctly. Students recognized how to calculate a percentage error, but
many made errors in substituting the values correctly. The majority forgot to add 4
and 14 to their answer for part (a).
HL:
The response to this question was generally sound, with many fully correct
attempts.
Part (a) was either fully correct or students floundered. Trapezoidal rule is a
standard technique that should be taught to all.
The indefinite integration was misinterpreted by some students- these giving the
numerical value of the area from 0 to 4. Others did not include the constant of
integration.
Part (c) was well attempted; the major error being a non-exact answer.
Where part (d) was interpreted correctly, great success was seen. Errors occurred
through not reading the question carefully enough.

value money (TVM) app on a calculator. It is important to understand that
for questions involving payments, the use of the compound interest formula will
yield incorrect results. The TVM application is essential for annuities/amortization.
Since interest is calculated at the end of a compounding period, a non-integer final
answer in part (c) was incorrect. Very few students were awarded full marks for the
final payment in part (d). The most common error seen in calculating the final
payment, were students incorrectly multiplying the new monthly payment by the
residual decimal value of n found in part (c). In part (e), students were most
successful when supporting their final answer with complete working.
HL:
It was clear that a surprising number of students were unable to use the financial
solver on their GDC, leading to many unsuccessful attempts at this question. Those
that used the solver, generally made some good attempts at parts (a) to (c). Few
students were able to recognize the subtlety of part (d) with some partial marks for
getting to the amount left owing after 291 months but failing to calculate the
interest for the final month. Many students were able to get "follow through" marks
for part (e).

parts.label: a
parts.q_text:
The company Fred Express delivers packages. From past experience, the time taken, T, to deliver a package
follows a normal distribution with mean 64 hours and standard deviation 12 hours.
(a) State P(T <64). [1]
parts.ms_text:
0.5 A1
[1 mark]
parts.report_text:
SL:
When finding P(T <64), some did not recognize the numerical limitations of their GDC, stating their
answer as 0.499999…or 0.5000000001.
The current generation of students are digital natives and so are more technologically literate. Most
students were able to perform routine tasks in their GDC. In part (b), P(44<T <64) was correct for
the majority of students. Errors in this part were usually attributed to an answer given to two significant
figures or interpretating the variable as discrete rather than continuous.
Most students drew a normal curve, though some poor sketches were seen. Common breaches in
tolerance included crude sketches with no change of curvature towards the extreme values, poor
symmetry, or not reflecting asymptotic properties of the curve. Students should support their diagram
with labelling of the mean and k. Most shaded the left-hand tail. It was encouraging to see many
students supporting their work with an attempt at working for the inverse function when finding k in
part (c)(ii).
Many did not recognize the binomial event in part (d). Those who did usually were rewarded with full
marks.
It was pleasing to see a few students find the correct expression for the amount charged to deliver a
package for x>1. The majority, however, did not consider the domain, incorrectly writing their
expression as 2x+4.5. On a positive note, students with an error in part (e) usually went on to score
follow-through marks in the subsequent parts of the question.
HL:
It was quite shocking to see the number of students that treated parts (a) and (b) as a discrete
distribution, leading to no marks in those parts. There were a significant number that gave 2sf answers
and even 1sf answers to these parts with the resultant loss of marks. Part (c) was generally much more
successfully attempted. Part (d) was the most difficult part of the question, but there was a pleasingly
high proportion of students achieving full marks on this. Part (e) was answered by many students as
2x+4.5, but the remaining parts were well answered by the majority of the students.

price of a single smoothie in pesos.

x2

[2 marks]
parts.report_text:
SL:
Most students picked up early marks finding the maximum price in part (a) and the number of
smoothies sold and total income in part (b).
The vast majority of students failed to make any headway with part (c), usually substituting in x=2
into the expression for P. The substituting of known values could at best satisfy a command term
'Verify' but is not generally appropriate in a 'Show that' question. A few students had modest success by
correctly multiplying the cost of each smoothie by the number of smoothies sold per day. Finding the
total revenue per day proved more problematic, with only the best student responses accruing full
marks.
It was pleasing to see many students attempt to express P with negative indices in readiness for the
power rule. Relative to past exams, more students were able to find the correct derivative. However, it is
clear that some students need more practice differentiating negative powers.
There were a surprising number of incorrect answers in parts (c)(iii) and (iv). Although follow-through
marks were awarded, some students lost marks for answers that were either negative or unrealistic.
HL:
Parts (a) and (b) were generally well answered. Part (c)(i) was very poorly attempted by many students,
although there were many good solutions to the rest of the question. It seems that students are not
prepared for a "show that" question where their steps need to be clearly explained. Many students
successfully differentiated the expression, although a surprising number of students treated it as two
separate applications of the quotient rule, increasing the chances of errors. Many students could
successfully find where that derivative equals zero, by a variety of different means. Many students
struggled to recognize which equation to substitute into and there were many calculation errors in part
(iv).

parts.report_text:
This question was found difficult by a number of candidates, even some who performed relatively well
on other questions. The initial part of the question caused the most problems, and the knock-on effect
was that candidates seemed to struggle on the relatively straight forward questions that came after it.
In part (a) quite a few candidates had problems setting out a clear demonstration of the formula to be
found. Candidates who used a diagrammatic method rarely drew an actual diagram in their answers,
and whilst still able to score full marks, it made the communication of their demonstration less
satisfactory. Despite some good responses, candidates showed a general lack of confidence in
successfully completing a "show that" arguments of this nature. In part (b) candidates who struggled to
respond to (a) seemed to have problems using the "show that" formula in (b). A significant number of
candidates used their incorrect formulae from part (a) in part (b). It seemed there was a lack of
understanding of what is meant by "dimensions" since quite a lot of candidates only found the valuse
of (cid:0). Also, candidates who found one set of dimensions in (b), often did not find both sets. This might
be due to candidates using nSolve() on their GDC and getting a unique solution. Parts (c), (d) and (e)
were quite well done, although some candidates who found (a) and (b) difficult seemed to lack the
confidence to attempt these question parts.

parts.report_text:
SL:
This was mostly well attempted, especially parts (a) and (b), where follow through (FT) marks were
commonly earned. Rounding to 2 sf caused some to miss the final mark. In part (c), few candidates
recognised the need to draw a perpendicular line from the point to the road. A number attempted area
methods or used Pythagoras’ theorem. The concept of shortest distance as perpendicular was often not
fully grasped.
HL:
Most candidates demonstrated a solid understanding of the sine and cosine rules in parts (a) and (b),
correctly applying the given side lengths and angle measures. However, a small number of candidates
made calculator errors by working in radian mode instead of degrees, which led to incorrect answers. This
was most likely due to the resetting of calculators which defaults to radian mode and is something that
candidates must be aware of. In part (c), a common misconception was evident in this part where many
candidates did not recognize that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance.
Instead, several attempted to calculate the distance to a median or an angle bisector, which was not
appropriate for the question.

Most students were able to find the point of intersection of the boundaries of the Voronoi
diagram, although some did not write their answer as a coordinate pair.

perpendicular bisector many students spent valuable time attempting with various degrees of success to
transform their linear equation y−8=−4(x−4) to another form such as 4x+5y−56=0. Some

calculator skills let students down in finding the correct answer at this point. In part (f), few students
appreciated that AC meant that B was not being used, which was not helped by students not labelling
their matrix satisfactorily.

SL TZ1:
Students who wrote down a correct ordered list of happiness scores leading to an incorrect upper
quartile were rewarded with one mark for correct working. This might also reveal that they were not

any knowledge of the outlier calculation for the upper fence. Some found both upper and lower fences.
This less efficient approach impacted the time a student might spend on other question parts.
Sometimes the calculation was correct, but the reasoning was vague and imprecise.
Stronger students generally performed well in part (c). However, errors suggest that many students are
uncertain about how to handle tied ranks, leading to incorrect results. In part (d)(i), it was disappointing

happiness score and happiness rank. These errors highlight a significant misunderstanding of the
concept and application of Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Part (e) was poorly answered.
Confusion with Pearson's product moment correlation coefficient was often seen, with 'weak
correlation of happiness score and country rank' as a common incorrect answer.

the time a student might spend on other question parts. Sometimes the calculation was correct, but

of the happiness score and country rank was incorrect. It is important the interpretation of r is precise

and refers to the 'linear correlation' between the ranks of the variables.

parts.report_text:
SL:
Almost all students were able to find the mid-interval value of the class, while the calculation of the
mean proved more problematic. Students who lost the mark in part (a)(i) usually considered the data as
discrete, while the most common error given for part (a)(ii) was the frequency value. Student answers
suggest the calculator was not set up correctly to use the frequencies as well as the data values. While
most were able to identify the quartiles, some only found the frequencies rather than the
measurements. Students should be taught that quartiles can also be found from a cumulative
frequency diagram or box and whisker plot and not just their GDC. The lack of accuracy in reading
values from the cumulative frequency graph is a concern. The students were usually successful in
assessing a possible outlier and justifying their reasoning. However, some were less efficient in their
solution, finding both the upper and lower fence for outliers.
The null and alternative hypotheses in the χ2 goodness of fit test were sometimes reversed.
Surprisingly, students struggled to phrase the hypotheses. The correct wording was given in the
question and should have been mirrored by students. Parameters of the distribution were often
omitted in one or both hypotheses. Some students confused this with a test for independence and
included "independent" in their hypotheses. It is insufficient to state "the expected and observed
frequencies are equal". Teachers should note the assumption of normality is only for the population
data and not the sample. The lack of scaffolding in part (e) was troubling for most students. Many were
not able to calculate the probability of normally distributed data and find associated expected values.
The lack of signposts should not be seen as an invitation to not show working. Students should be
encouraged to state the degrees of freedom, write down the p-value and then explicitly state the
numerical comparison. Students should be able to interpret the results of a statistical test and be able
to communicate this in the context of the question.
HL:
It was very surprising just how many students were unable to correctly answer (a)(ii). The most
common answer was 175 obtained by ignoring the frequencies altogether. In addition, it was
surprising how many students used a formula to calculate the mean, rather than their GDC. Again, for
part (b), surprisingly few students could find the interquartile range from a cumulative frequency curve.
Two parts were fundamental to statistics, in a course where statistics has a major part. In part (c), a
generous markscheme allowed many students to achieve partial marks, but few were able to obtain full
marks because of not knowing how to find the upper fence.
Part (d) showed that many students had some idea as to what they should be doing, but
unfortunately were unable to complete these hypotheses correctly. Many did not include the
parameters as part of the hypotheses and, once again, many had the hypotheses the wrong way round.
In addition, many students spoke of the sample being normally distributed, rather than the underlying
population. Part (e) was relatively well answered in general.

The gardener in a local park suggested that the number of snails found in the park can be modelled by a
Poisson distribution.

parts.report_text:
This was, on the whole, a well answered question with most candidates having some success, although
very few managed full marks. In part (a) candidates did not seem familiar with the assumptions and
conditions required for a Poisson distribution or did not interpret the question as asking about this.
Although many candidates got at least one of the two marks available with responses well spread
between the different potential correct answers. Part (b) was well done with the majority of candidates
using 2.4 as the correct mean. In part (e) candidates were generally familiar with the concept of
hypothesis testing in this context. However, many candidates did not use the mean of the number of
snails in their hypotheses, but rather talked about numbers of snails, which is incorrect. In part (f)
candidates were not always able to transfer their correct working into a correctly written interval that
represented the Critical Region. Part (g) had plenty of good attempts on this quite challenging problem
on Type II errors.

parts.report_text:
The response to part (a) was mixed. A large number of candidates made a common error of adding
the two standard deviations, instead of the correct method of adding the variances. This seemed to
indicate a lack of familiarity with linear combinations, despite it being a fairly standard exam question.
In part (b), common errors included multiplying the standard deviation by 8 or multiplying the variance
by 64. Part (c)(i) was answered well, but many candidates could not interpret the correct value on their
GDC to answer (c)(ii). In part (d) many candidates were able to score some marks, but only the strongest
candidates could obtain the correct p-value.
